text.p: Canada has delivered yet another exemplary fiscal budget but the outperformance of its bond market against its dollar bloc cousins has reached a brick wall, analysts said on Wednesday.

There may be gains at the ultra long end of the curve, but robust Canadian growth in 1997 has the potential to start nudging up interest rates, making Australian and U.S. bonds a better bet in price terms.
"There is not much value in the Canadian bond market," said Dick Howard, senior economist at Julius Baer Investments here. "It's well through the U.S. all the way to around 20 years."
Overseas analysts were certainly pleased with the 1997/98 budget delivered on Tuesday.

Finance Minister Paul Martin predicted Canada's deficit for fiscal 1996/97 would be no more than C$19 billion, way below an original projection of C$24.3 billion and the third straight year Martin has beaten his deficit targets.
The 1997/98 deficit was seen falling to C$17 billion.

But international investors are getting used to good budget news from Canada and have bought bonds heavily -- helping to squeeze the yield spread between 10-year Canadian and U.S. bonds to around minus 14 basis points from a recent peak of around 177 basis points in August 1995.
The 10-year spread has been static in the last few months, hovering around parity since October last year. Analysts do not see it moving much deeper from here.
Howard at Julius Baer said the Bank of Canada would not be able to keep interest rates at 40-year lows much longer, with most economic indicators showing strong signs of revival.
Finance Minister Martin said in the budget Canada's economy would grow by 3.2 percent in 1997. That would make it one of the fastest growing of the Group of Seven industrialised countries.
Meanwhile, its key interest rate is at 3.25 percent and its call rate range at 2.75 to 3.25 percent.

"The scope for Canadian interest rates to rise this year is significantly higher than for U.S. rates to rise," said Howard. He expected U.S. rates to go up by 25 to 50 basis points and Canadian rates by around 100 to bring Canadian monetary policy back to a more neutral stance.
Howard said the Canada/U.S. 10-year spread was more fairly valued at around 50 basis points over.

He said Australian bonds offered better value at around its current 105 basis points over U.S. 10-years. The Reserve Bank has made it clear chances of an interest rate cut have all but disappeared but growth was not going to run away in 1997 and inflation was expected to be reasonable.

Sonja Gibbs, senior market strategist at Nomura International in London, liked Treasuries better. She expected U.S. growth to slow and a burgeoning dollar to crimp inflation, pushing long term U.S. Treasury yields toward 5.75 percent by the end of the year from around 6.50 percent now.
The Canada/U.S. spread was likely to remain in a range of around minus 25 basis points to 50 basis points over through much of the year, but the risk was to the downside.
"All the good news in the domestic front in Canada is factored in," she said.
Miguel Array, a director of fixed income at Matheson Securities in Jersey, was more optimistic on Canadian bonds.
He said more value could be squeezed out of the long end of the curve and saw the 30-year spread to slimming to parity from around 28 basis points over now.
The fiscal drag of a severe budget and high unemployment will make the Bank of Canada think twice before raising interest rates, he said.
